Scholar Transport- Long Walk To School

By: Sophia Phirippides | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

Unique Selling Point:
There are over 1 million children in need of scholar transport in the country with some in the rural areas having to walk over 14 Kilometres Just to make it to class and back home. Is the safety of these pupil and their rights neglected?




Summary:
Since 2014 activists from Equal Education have been advocating and campaigning for scholar transport for children in Kwa-Zulu Natal. For many children in rural KZN, getting to school means waking up in the wee hours of the morning and embarking on a long two and half hours walk just to get an education.

These routes that they take are quite dangerous as the children run the risks of drowning in the rivers they have to cross or even get raped or abducted. The department of education in KZN has cried budgetary constraints to assist these learners with transport while nationally there was a promise from the minister to allocate grants for scholar transport but nothing has been forth coming.

A court ruling in KZN was in favour of EE and has now forced the department of education in KZN to provide transport for this students and has given them a deadline of 1st April 2018 to present to the court a report that outlines how they will accommodate and assist all the children that are in need of scholar transport in KZN.

The use of private scholar transport such as bakkies and mini taxis has also endangered the lives of the children as Omalume (drivers of private scholar transport) constantly overload their vehicles for extra money at the expense of these children’s lives. The department of transport has put out a law that prohibits the Omalume to transport school children but according to Jabulani Dladla from the KZN scholar transport association, business is still running smoothly in KZN atleats until January whilst they are still in negotiations with the department to help them acquire new vehicles that meet the regulatory standards.


Further information:
Luyolo Mazwambe from Equal Education, is part of the EE team that took KZN department of Education to court regarding 12 schools whose student have had to travel over 3KM to get to class in Nquthu village. The court ruled in favour of EE and the twelve schools but also requested for the department to make a plan and give a report by 1st April 2018 that they will provide answers to how they plan to provide transport for all scholars who qualify for it in KZN( Any child that travels 3KM on foot). He will share how far they have come with the case. According to Luyolo the government had said it would cost them about R4 Billion to provide transport for all children who need it across KZN. He believes bakkies are a hazard to children’s safety. They Demand roadworthy buses for the children and qualified drivers as part of the Government solution. He knows the children personally and the schools the children attend as well as their parents



Nombulelo Vilakazi is a 17 year old school girl who attends grade 11 at Zixole high school. Her case is quite sensitive as she was raped on one of her long journeys to school. Fortunately she was able to identify the culprit and he was arrested. She walks 5 Kilometres to school and she crosses two valleys to get there. She was raped on the second one. Her issue is that her parents don’t know that she was raped and she would like to keep it that way.


Nkosientle Sibisi and Sifiso Sibis (not siblings) is a grade 11 pupil who has to travel 14 Kilometres to school in the rural Nquthu area of KZN. He attends at Hlubi high school, according Equal Education Nkosientle attends next to a primary school whose pupils are afforded transport but he can’t use the same transport because he is in high school. (Still need to contact him)


Jabulani Dladla, Spokeperson of KZN scholar Transport Association says they are still negotiations with the government with regard to the new law that prohibits them from transporting pupils for money. According to Mr Dladla Business is still running smooth and they have not been affected yet but the agreement that they have with their members is that by January they need to have all moved to minibuses. There will be no more bakkies. They are trying to negotiate with government to assist with buying the minibuses, as they cannot afford them. Dladla says the issue of safety is puzzling to him because anybody can have an accident. Whether they’re driving a bakkie or a minibus.

MEC of Education in KZN Mr Mthandeni Dlugwane will also speak to Carte Blanche to outline how they plan to go about providing scholar transport to all the children in need. Most importantly why did it take the court to force them into action while children were drowning in rivers and some being raped on their way to school?

Mr Mxolisi Kaunda, MEC of transport, community safety and liason in KZN will speak to the dangers that the bakkie transport system and the unlicensed vehicles are still on the road in KZN transporting children whilst the is a law that prohibits them to do so.

The fact remains these children should have had to go through this and the department has let them down. Is their safety secondary, Carte Blanche investigates.


Extra Budget Items:
Travel and Accommodation. We would need a 4x4 vehicle to travel the rural KZN. We also need a drone to be able to show and emphasize the distances covered by these learners to get to school

Press Release:


There are over 1 million children in need of scholar transport in South Africa, with some in the rural areas having to walk over 14 kilometres just to make it to class and back home. Is the safety of these pupils and their rights being neglected?

Script:


LINK: Many children in the most rural parts of South Africa have to wake up in the early hours of the morning to walk distances of 10km or more just to get to school every day in total darkness and battle terrain like this, some of them have been robbed others have been raped and some have died

“Nonhlanhla”: It was in April on my way from home, to school. It was cold that day and I was walking. That person was always watching me me all the time after school and I always saw him just sitting there. Then once on my way to school he grabbed me. //BEAT//And that's when he raped me.

VO: Nonhlanhla, (not her real name), a 17 year old school girl has never told anyone in her family about her dark secret, she says the circumstances at home are too difficult, but this is the price she has to pay for going to school.

“Nonhlanhla”:I was not the only one because a friend of mine, she was also raped and unfortunately, they killed her. She died right there.

VO: Nonhlanhla lives on the outskirts of Nqutu in rural KZN, She wakes up at 4am to get ready and then begins her daily trek to school, about a one and a half hour walk and over 5 kilometers, through valleys and mountains and often in treacherous weather conditions. Since the incident she says she's had to learn to live with her ordeal.

“Nonhlanhla”: I let it pass. I kept on reading books everyday, newspapers, even movies about what it's like to be raped. I learned there that the trauma will always be there. I chose to continue with my life.

VO: The MEC for Basic Education in KwaZulu-Natal Mthandeni Dlungwana, is disturbed by what is happening, and says that government has to take responsibility for the safety of it's learners.

Dlungwana: When I took over as MEC for education in 2016 the first incident was 1 girl raped and killed in Insinga. I was in pain because I'm a parent, I myself come from a rural area, I know the environment and situation.

VO: According to Research by International Budget Partnership for 2017 and 2018, there are in excess of 1 million children in need of transport to school nationwide, and KZN is the province with the highest number of learners walking to school. Luyolo Mazweme, National organiser for Equal Education says they are fighting on behalf of children who's rights are being violated.

Luyolo: Learners have been struck by lightning. There's been cases where learners get kidnapped.

VO: Sifiso Sibisi, a grade 11 pupil walks over 14 kilometers to school and back every day. He fears for his 9 year old brother who has to walk part of the journey alone.

Sifiso: We have to cross through Nkanjeni. there are criminals at Nkanjeni in the evenings.

Mac: What do they do to you?

Sifiso: They take us and leave with us.

Mac: And then?

Sifiso: They kill you

Mac: Kill you for what?

Sifiso: I don't know. because that did happen that one child was cut up. head separated from the body. I don't know why they do that or what they want.

Luyolo: Some parents who are tired of this situation. They hire out taxis and bakkies which cost R350 a month. Most of these vehicles that are being used are unroadworthy vehicles. They're being driven by drivers without licenses, some of them don't even have seat belts to protect these learners.

VO: The desperate need for safe and accessible transport for learners was brought to the fore last year when a number of horrific taxi and bakkie accidents occurred. Over 12 learners were killed in unroadworthy and overloaded vehicles in KwaZulu-Natal alone.

Cyprian Dladla, is the treasurer of Santaco for KZN, which transports school children in bakkies, taxis and buses,

Cyprian: The problem is when you're carrying 15 children even though we don’t support overload, we cannot afford to pay the installment.

Luyolo: Getting more learners in a bakkie means more business for them and the quicker you go and drop these ones at these school and then go and pick up these ones at the other school you're making more money for yourself.

VO: Santaco say they can't police what they cannot see, but Bakkies have been in use since the 1990's.

Cyprian: Some of the roads are gravel so theres no alternative, they must use the bakkies.

Luyolo: Parents are forced to risk their children's lives because they're tired of their learners who are waking up early in the morning and coming back very late so they end up risking put them in these bakkies.

Mac: Tell me how much does it cost you for transport?

Sifiso: It's R15 OR R10. Some families do not have the money. So the kids don't have a problem walking because they've got used to it.
VO: Equal Education has been campaigning for scholar transport in Nqutu KZN, since 2014, where the situation is desperate. 12 schools with about 4000 learners in need were submitted to the Department of Basic Education, but only 7 of them qualified.

Luyolo: Five of these schools do not qualify and the reason to that is because they're are schools of choice and that means that learners are deciding to leave schools that are close to them and go to further schools.

Luyolo: The department is not obliged to provide scholar transport to schools of choice. But that is not true because we went on the ground, these schools are schools of need, but the fact is that the school are far.

VO: The National policy stipulates that children who walk 5 kilometers or more should have access to transport. Equal Education was not going to take this lying down, and took the Department to court Finally they had an outcome in November last year.

LINK: The court ruled that the Department of Education and the Department of Transport has to provide scholar transport for 12 schools in Nqutu area by April 1st 2018

Dlungwana: I'm concerned, that matter does not belong to court. It is our responsibility to provide learner transport.

Luyolo:This is just 12 schools that's gonna recieve scholar transport. So it won't eradicate the problem.

LINK: There are 90 000 learners that are in need of scholar transport in Kwazulu Natal but that number is far more, Currently only 47 000 have been catered for, the department says they need more than 400 million just to cater for these 90 000 learners

Dlungwana: We are having a budget of R195 million the province had to add another R105 million. Even with that additional 105 million its not enough.

VO: But the International Budget Partnership research, shows a much bleaker picture for KZN, with over 300 000 scholars needing transport to school.

Dlungwana: We are also doing our own assessment That research could be correct, but we can only see the figures once we get the assessments back. We are looking at over 400 million with the 90 000 learners but the need is more.

Macfarlane: How are you going to be able to meet the need if you're already struggling?

Dlungwana: We hope we get additional funding to provide transport to more learners. I hope other partners will come on board.

VO: According to the auditor general's report which was published last year, the KZN Department of Education irregularly spent 820 Million Rand, more than double what is needed to transport learners. The MEC says it happened before his tenure.

Dlungwana: The current issue is we are transporting less with more money. We can design the system to transport more with less.

VO: At the moment buses are stationary at schools between pick ups, whereas they could be used to transport other commuters.

LINK: The SANTACO Taxi Association for Scholar Transport in KwaZulu-Natal is adamant that they can help with the dire need of scholar transport in the province.

Cyprian: We understand if they don't want bakkies but we want the government to come forward to help us because when it comes to minibuses, its not easy to buy them.

Macfarlane: A survey says theres 300 000 children who need transport, can you handle all of that?

Cyprian: If we know exactly how many children need transport definitely Shure!

Luyolo: According to the DBE in their measures, the budget for everyone in South Africa for everyone is R3.7 Billion for scholar transport but since this recent research points out that the figures that are given out are not actually the correct figures so that research is pushing up the number to R7 Billion.

VO: The impact for scholars walking long distances to school has far reaching effects, beyond even their immediate safety.

“Nonhlanhla”: If you've walked a long distance, you don't have focus at school, especially when it's raining, you arrive wet, the books are wet and the teachers are shouting at you and beat you up for your books being wet. It's not easy.

Mac: So when you come back you walk again another 7 Km late. What do you do when you get home?

Sifiso: I arrive tired. I have to go gather the cattle.

Luyolo: Everyone is expecting this matrics to pass well so that they can go to university,how is that gonna be possible when there is all these challenges in front of them?

VO: But these children are determined more than ever to get an education as they continue to brave the valleys and the planes on their long walk to school.

Luyolo Mazweme, National organiser for Equal Education says they are fighting on behalf of children who's rights are being violated. Luyolo: Learners have been struck by lightning. There's been cases where learners get kidnapped. VO: Sifiso Sibisi, a grade 11 pupil walks over 14 kilometers to school and back every day. He fears for his 9 year old brother who has to walk part of the journey alone. Sifiso: We have to cross through Nkanjeni. there are criminals at Nkanjeni in the evenings. Mac: What do they do to you? Sifiso: They take us and leave with us. Mac: And then? Sifiso: They kill you Mac: Kill you for what? Sifiso: I don't know. because that did happen that one child was cut up. head separated from the body. I don't know why they do that or what they want. Luyolo: Some parents who are tired of this situation. They hire out taxis and bakkies which cost R350 a month. Most of these vehicles that are being used are unroadworthy vehicles. They're being driven by drivers without licenses, some of them don't even have seat belts to protect these learners. VO: The desperate need for safe and accessible transport for learners was brought to the fore last year when a number of horrific taxi and bakkie accidents occurred. Over 12 learners were killed in unroadworthy and overloaded vehicles in KwaZulu-Natal alone. Cyprian Dladla, is the treasurer of Santaco for KZN, which transports school children in bakkies, taxis and buses, Cyprian: The problem is when you're carrying 15 children even though we don’t support overload, we cannot afford to pay the installment. Luyolo: Getting more learners in a bakkie means more business for them and the quicker you go and drop these ones at these school and then go and pick up these ones at the other school you're making more money for yourself. VO: Santaco say they can't police what they cannot see, but Bakkies have been in use since the 1990's. Cyprian: Some of the roads are gravel so theres no alternative, they must use the bakkies. Luyolo: Parents are forced to risk their children's lives because they're tired of their learners who are waking up early in the morning and coming back very late so they end up risking put them in these bakkies. Mac: Tell me how much does it cost you for transport? Sifiso: It's R15 OR R10. Some families do not have the money. So the kids don't have a problem walking because they've got used to it. VO: Equal Education has been campaigning for scholar transport in Nqutu KZN, since 2014, where the situation is desperate. 12 schools with about 4000 learners in need were submitted to the Department of Basic Education, but only 7 of them qualified. Luyolo: Five of these schools do not qualify and the reason to that is because they're are schools of choice and that means that learners are deciding to leave schools that are close to them and go to further schools. Luyolo: The department is not obliged to provide scholar transport to schools of choice. But that is not true because we went on the ground, these schools are schools of need, but the fact is that the school are far. VO: The National policy stipulates that children who walk 5 kilometers or more should have access to transport. Equal Education was not going to take this lying down, and took the Department to court Finally they had an outcome in November last year. LINK: The court ruled that the Department of Education and the Department of Transport has to provide scholar transport for 12 schools in Nqutu area by April 1st 2018 Dlungwana: I'm concerned, that matter does not belong to court. It is our responsibility to provide learner transport. Luyolo:This is just 12 schools that's gonna recieve scholar transport. So it won't eradicate the problem. LINK: There are 90 000 learners that are in need of scholar transport in Kwazulu Natal but that number is far more, Currently only 47 000 have been catered for, the department says they need more than 400 million just to cater for these 90 000 learners Dlungwana: We are having a budget of R195 million the province had to add another R105 million. Even with that additional 105 million its not enough. VO: But the International Budget Partnership research, shows a much bleaker picture for KZN, with over 300 000 scholars needing transport to school. Dlungwana: We are also doing our own assessment That research could be correct, but we can only see the figures once we get the assessments back. We are looking at over 400 million with the 90 000 learners but the need is more. Macfarlane: How are you going to be able to meet the need if you're already struggling? Dlungwana: We hope we get additional funding to provide transport to more learners. I hope other partners will come on board. VO: According to the auditor general's report which was published last year, the KZN Department of Education irregularly spent 820 Million Rand, more than double what is needed to transport learners. The MEC says it happened before his tenure. Dlungwana: The current issue is we are transporting less with more money. We can design the system to transport more with less. VO: At the moment buses are stationary at schools between pick ups, whereas they could be used to transport other commuters. LINK: The SANTACO Taxi Association for Scholar Transport in KwaZulu-Natal is adamant that they can help with the dire need of scholar transport in the province. Cyprian: We understand if they don't want bakkies but we want the government to come forward to help us because when it comes to minibuses, its not easy to buy them. Macfarlane: A survey says theres 300 000 children who need transport, can you handle all of that? Cyprian: If we know exactly how many children need transport definitely Shure! Luyolo: According to the DBE in their measures, the budget for everyone in South Africa for everyone is R3.7 Billion for scholar transport but since this recent research points out that the figures that are given out are not actually the correct figures so that research is pushing up the number to R7 Billion. VO: The impact for scholars walking long distances to school has far reaching effects, beyond even their immediate safety. “Nonhlanhla”: If you've walked a long distance, you don't have focus at school, especially when it's raining, you arrive wet, the books are wet and the teachers are shouting at you and beat you up for your books being wet. It's not easy. Mac: So when you come back you walk again another 7 Km late. What do you do when you get home? Sifiso: I arrive tired. I have to go gather the cattle. Luyolo: Everyone is expecting this matrics to pass well so that they can go to university,how is that gonna be possible when there is all these challenges in front of them? VO: But these children are determined more than ever to get an education as they continue to brave the valleys and the planes on their long walk to school.

metadata.Unique Selling Point: There are over 1 million children in need of scholar transport in the country with some in the rural areas having to walk over 14 Kilometres Just to make it to class and back home. Is the safety of these pupil and their rights neglected?
metadata.Summary: Since 2014 activists from Equal Education have been advocating and campaigning for scholar transport for children in Kwa-Zulu Natal. For many children in rural KZN, getting to school means waking up in the wee hours of the morning and embarking on a long two and half hours walk just to get an education. These routes that they take are quite dangerous as the children run the risks of drowning in the rivers they have to cross or even get raped or abducted. The department of education in KZN has cried budgetary constraints to assist these learners with transport while nationally there was a promise from the minister to allocate grants for scholar transport but nothing has been forth coming. A court ruling in KZN was in favour of EE and has now forced the department of education in KZN to provide transport for this students and has given them a deadline of 1st April 2018 to present to the court a report that outlines how they will accommodate and assist all the children that are in need of scholar transport in KZN. The use of private scholar transport such as bakkies and mini taxis has also endangered the lives of the children as Omalume (drivers of private scholar transport) constantly overload their vehicles for extra money at the expense of these children’s lives. The department of transport has put out a law that prohibits the Omalume to transport school children but according to Jabulani Dladla from the KZN scholar transport association, business is still running smoothly in KZN atleats until January whilst they are still in negotiations with the department to help them acquire new vehicles that meet the regulatory standards.
metadata.Further information: Luyolo Mazwambe from Equal Education, is part of the EE team that took KZN department of Education to court regarding 12 schools whose student have had to travel over 3KM to get to class in Nquthu village. The court ruled in favour of EE and the twelve schools but also requested for the department to make a plan and give a report by 1st April 2018 that they will provide answers to how they plan to provide transport for all scholars who qualify for it in KZN( Any child that travels 3KM on foot). He will share how far they have come with the case. According to Luyolo the government had said it would cost them about R4 Billion to provide transport for all children who need it across KZN. He believes bakkies are a hazard to children’s safety. They Demand roadworthy buses for the children and qualified drivers as part of the Government solution. He knows the children personally and the schools the children attend as well as their parents Nombulelo Vilakazi is a 17 year old school girl who attends grade 11 at Zixole high school. Her case is quite sensitive as she was raped on one of her long journeys to school. Fortunately she was able to identify the culprit and he was arrested. She walks 5 Kilometres to school and she crosses two valleys to get there. She was raped on the second one. Her issue is that her parents don’t know that she was raped and she would like to keep it that way. Nkosientle Sibisi and Sifiso Sibis (not siblings) is a grade 11 pupil who has to travel 14 Kilometres to school in the rural Nquthu area of KZN. He attends at Hlubi high school, according Equal Education Nkosientle attends next to a primary school whose pupils are afforded transport but he can’t use the same transport because he is in high school. (Still need to contact him) Jabulani Dladla, Spokeperson of KZN scholar Transport Association says they are still negotiations with the government with regard to the new law that prohibits them from transporting pupils for money. According to Mr Dladla Business is still running smooth and they have not been affected yet but the agreement that they have with their members is that by January they need to have all moved to minibuses. There will be no more bakkies. They are trying to negotiate with government to assist with buying the minibuses, as they cannot afford them. Dladla says the issue of safety is puzzling to him because anybody can have an accident. Whether they’re driving a bakkie or a minibus. MEC of Education in KZN Mr Mthandeni Dlugwane will also speak to Carte Blanche to outline how they plan to go about providing scholar transport to all the children in need. Most importantly why did it take the court to force them into action while children were drowning in rivers and some being raped on their way to school? Mr Mxolisi Kaunda, MEC of transport, community safety and liason in KZN will speak to the dangers that the bakkie transport system and the unlicensed vehicles are still on the road in KZN transporting children whilst the is a law that prohibits them to do so. The fact remains these children should have had to go through this and the department has let them down. Is their safety secondary, Carte Blanche investigates.
